Welcome to **Développement d'applications internet (DAI)**!

## What this course is about

The Internet runs on programs talking to each other. In this course you
will learn to build them:

- **Network programming** (inputs/outputs, encodings, TCP and UDP) —
  write client–server applications with the Socket API, from the bytes
  up.
- **Application-level protocols** (SMTP, SSH, HTTP… and your own) —
  understand the protocols the Internet runs on, then design one
  yourself.
- **Web infrastructures** (reverse proxy, load balancer, sticky
  sessions) — deploy your applications the way they run in production.
- **Reading and writing technical documentation** — the skill behind all
  the others: specifications, READMEs, and the reports you will write.

At the end of the course, you will be able to create applications that
communicate over the network — business applications, APIs, games,
anything.

Along the way you will adopt the tools of professional software
development: Git and GitHub, Docker, Maven, the terminal — the same
workflow you will use in industry.

## How the course works

Each week combines a **cours** (theory, kept short) and a **labo**
(practice — most of your learning happens here). The
[schedule](../index.qmd) maps every week to its content for your class.

- **Chapters** hold the material: theory, exercises with solutions, and a
  collapsible *Go further* section for the curious — the core content is
  what evaluations cover.
- **Practical works (PW)** are group projects spanning several weeks —
  they anchor the theory in something real, and you choose your own
  subject (we validate the idea).
- All communication happens in one place: the course
  [GitHub Discussions]({{< var discussions-url >}}) — questions, answers,
  announcements. There is no Cyberlearn, no Teams. Ask anything; there
  are no stupid questions.

The material is in English — the language of the field — while classes
and evaluations are in French. Course content may be improved during the
semester; we will tell you when something important changes.

## Grading

$$
\text{final grade} = \underbrace{(\text{TE1} \times 0.4 + \text{TE2} \times 0.6)}_{\text{cours}} \times\ 0.8\ +\ \underbrace{\text{PW}}_{\text{labo}} \times\ 0.2
$$

- **TE1** — mid-term evaluation, week 7, covers chapters 01–07.
- **TE2** — final evaluation, week 16, covers the whole semester.
- **PW** — the average of your three practical works, each graded on its
  report and deliverables (rubrics published with each PW).

There is no exam session exam — everything happens during the semester.

## AI tools

<!-- TODO(review): Olivier's AI policy — placeholder based on last year's
     spirit ("on ne se voile pas la face", best practices over bans) -->

AI assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, …) exist and you will use them
in your career — pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Ground rules:

- Use them to **understand** — explain an error, explore an approach —
  rather than to produce work you cannot explain.
- You are accountable for everything you submit: if you cannot explain
  your code line by line, it is not your code.
- Evaluations happen without AI assistance — if you let it do the
  learning, it will show there.

## Your week-1 checklist

1. Environment ready? Every verification of
   [chapter 00](00-environment-setup.qmd) passes. If something resists,
   this week is the moment to ask.
2. Accept the invitation to the course GitHub organization
   ({{< var org >}}).
3. Complete [chapter 02 — Git, GitHub & Markdown](02-git-github.qmd), including the
   SSH and signed-commits setup: everything else this semester builds on
   it.
